title: Bifur-circuits: Interactive and Modular Metamaterial Building Blocks Via Bifurcated Geometries.
abstract: Mechanical metamaterials have gained traction in the HCI community for enabling interactive applications, including shape-changing displays and novel sensing paradigms. However, these structures typically support a limited set of stable geometric configurations, constraining the range of geometric expressions they can support through modularity. To overcome this constraint, we present Bifur-circuits, a mechanically and electrically modular, fully 3D metamaterial assembly toolkit. Bifur-circuits enables interactive geometries capable of exhibiting an exponentially increasing number of configurations as a function of units in an assembly. It accomplishes this through two layers of mechanical reconfiguration: at the assembly level, where modules can be added or removed, and at the configuration level via mechanical bifurcation, where structures split into new stable configurations upon reaching a critical geometric threshold. All units are internally routed such that electrical modularity produces a valid and unique circuit per configuration. We contribute a Fusion 360-based construction tool, a Java-C++ simulation tool for real-time shape recognition, and a multi-material 3D printing fabrication pipeline. Our technical evaluation shows that Bifur-circuits maintain electrical connectivity after 10k cyclic compressions, and that shape recognition latency scales linearly with unit count (20 units maps to a 5-second detection time). Finally, we contribute two applications demonstrating Bifur-circuits’ potential, across scales, for reconfigurable spatial environments and adaptive tangible user interfaces.
conference_title: ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology

title: Sticki: Personalized Content Moderation Using Image Overlays for Recontextualizing Aversive Videos.
abstract: As digital content consumption increases, users are frequently exposed to aversive stimuli. Yet, conventional moderation methods often disrupt content context by obscuring objects and do not account for individual sensitivity. To address this, we present Sticki, a context-preserving moderation framework that supports reappraisal of aversive objects through animated image overlays. Sticki also enables users to select moderation targets and methods before exposure, supporting autonomy and psychological comfort. In a user study with 32 participants using surveys and interviews, Sticki achieved a better balance between two goals (i.e., disgust reduction and context preservation) than conventional methods. Sticki also provides users with a greater sense of autonomy and psychological comfort. We further discuss how individual sensitivity and viewing motivation shape users’ prioritization between the two goals, with implications for personalized content moderation system design.
conference_title: ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology

title: MolecularCanvas: LLM-assisted Small-Molecule Drug Discovery via Structure-Guided Constraints.
abstract: Small-molecule drug discovery relies on iterative molecular optimization, where chemists repeatedly modify candidate compounds to balance multiple competing properties such as efficacy, toxicity, and solubility. Recent advances in generative AI (GenAI), have shown promise in accelerating this process by automatically proposing new molecular structures or targeted modifications. However, existing GenAI-based molecular design tools remain poorly aligned with experts’ real-world workflows. Specifically, they offer limited support for specifying structure-level modification intents on molecules, provide insufficient transparency into model-generated modifications, and lack integrated support for downstream property evaluation with external computational tools. To address these challenges, we introduce MolecularCanvas, an interactive system that enables users to iteratively construct an optimization context by integrating high-level goals, structure-level annotations, property constraints, and reference-based preferences. This context guides the generation of candidate molecules across diverse molecular structures. MolecularCanvas further enhances transparency by providing evidence for AI-generated suggestions, and streamlines molecular evaluation by integrating commonly used property computational tools into a unified interface. Finally, a user study with 12 participants demonstrates the usefulness and effectiveness of MolecularCanvas in helping users optimize candidate molecules.
conference_title: ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology

title: Programmable Machine-Knitted Sensors for Deformable Interfaces.
abstract: Knitted textiles are well suited to wearable sensing because they are soft, conform to the body, and remain comfortable during wear. Industrial knitting also allows sensing layouts to be defined digitally. We present a programmable machine-knitted capacitive sensing substrate for wearable deformation sensing. The substrate realizes five functional layers through three physical knitted layers, with conductive yarn stripes and dielectric regions formed directly during knitting. The same sensing structure can be adapted to different wearable forms by modifying the knit pattern, which we demonstrate with elbow and shoulder prototypes. To evaluate how well the fabric captures deformation, we reconstruct the deforming fabric surface from spatial capacitance patterns using synchronized motion capture as supervision. We compare five model families under a six-fold leave-one-session-out protocol, with a Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) representing the field-based family. FNO and ConvLSTM achieve the lowest elbow reconstruction errors; on the shoulder, FNO has the lowest fabric-only mean and median error, while ConvLSTM does not improve over the single-frame baselines. These comparisons show that the relative value of spatial, temporal, and auxiliary pose representations depends on the wearable form. Surface reconstruction provides a shared geometric basis for evaluating programmable knitted deformation sensors across body regions.
conference_title: ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology

title: KnitARobo: Industrial Machine Knitting of Electromechanical Textile Interfaces with Liquid Crystal Elastomer Fibers.
abstract: Electromechanical textiles combine the unique properties of controllable shape-changing materials with the affordances of conventional fabrics. However, most actuation mechanisms require bespoke fabrication techniques incompatible with mass manufacturing. We present KnitARobo, a technique for automatically machine-knitting liquid-crystal elastomer textile actuators. Parameterized variations in the knitting pattern produce various morphologies. By characterizing these actuators and demonstrating three morphing garments, we demonstrate the value of our three guiding principles for electromechanical textile design: clothing-centric design, compatibility with mass manufacturing, and integration of controllable actuation.
conference_title: ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology

title: HALO: Interactive Co-abductive Reasoning in Hypothesis Generation for Scientific Discovery.
abstract: Scientific discovery is essential yet inefficient, primarily because generating hypotheses within a vast search space hinders breakthroughs. While current AI systems assist in generating new hypothesis candidates, they lack interactive support for the reasoning process by which users develop these outputs into promising hypotheses, resulting in surface-level hypotheses. To address this issue, we present a co-abduction, a human-AI collaborative framework for abductive reasoning in scientific hypothesis generation. To operationalize co-abduction, we build HALO, a human–AI collaborative system for molecular hypothesis generation in drug discovery, enabling improved candidate clustering, strategy identification, and multi-strategy synthesis. In expert studies involving 10 medicinal chemists, HALO significantly facilitated abductive reasoning for hypothesis generation—efficient candidate observation, systematic strategy identification, and coherent multi-strategy composition—and enabled participants to produce higher-quality, more diverse candidate molecules.
conference_title: ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology

title: WhatIf: Interactive Exploration of Large-Scale LLM Agent Simulations for Policy Reasoning.
abstract: Policymakers in domains such as emergency management, public health, and urban planning must make decisions under deep uncertainty, where outcomes depend on how large populations interpret information, coordinate, and adopt over time. Existing tools only partially support this process: tabletop exercises enable collaborative discussion but lack dynamic feedback, while computational simulations capture population dynamics but are designed for offline analysis. We present WhatIf, an interactive system that enables policymakers to steer, inspect, and compare LLM-powered social simulations in real time. Informed by a formative study in emergency preparedness planning, we derive four design requirements for interactive policy simulations: fluid steering, real-time scale, collaborative exploration, and multi-level interpretability. We developed WhatIf guided by these requirements and evaluated it with five preparedness professionals across three disaster evacuation scenarios. Our findings show that participants used the system as a space for iterative branching and comparison rather than evaluating fixed plans; reflected on tacit planning assumptions when agent behavior violated expectations; surfaced previously unrecognized planning vulnerabilities; and grounded their reasoning in inspectable agent-level cases rather than aggregate outputs alone. These findings suggest broader design implications for LLM-powered social simulation systems: designing such systems as interactive, shared reasoning environments—rather than offline predictive tools—can better support expert decision-making under deep uncertainty.
conference_title: ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology

title: MetaBeads: Enabling Shape- and Stiffness-Changing Interfaces through Beaded Metamaterials.
abstract: As interactive systems increasingly extend into the physical world, designers need accessible ways to prototype interfaces that can change both shape and stiffness. In this paper, we investigate how simple, widely available materials—beads and string—can be used to construct shape- and stiffness-changing interfaces without specialized machinery. We introduce a set of reusable structural mechanisms that enable sturdy, wearable, and load-bearing structures from bead-based assemblies, each supporting a distinct mode of deformation and stiffness change, such as transforming from a flexible sheet into a jammed cuboid, a stiff tube, or a bistable curvature cell. To facilitate the creation of these structures, we provide an interactive design tool that guides craftspeople designing and fabricating their own MetaBead interfaces. We demonstrate the possibilities of MetaBeads through four application prototypes across wearable devices, educational tools, and adaptive furniture. Together, this work offers an accessible approach to prototyping shape- and stiffness-changing interfaces with everyday materials.
conference_title: ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology

title: ShadAR: Real-time Prompting On-demand Visual Augmentation in Augmented Reality.
abstract: Augmented Reality can reshape our visual perception (e.g., simulating color blindness) yet such effects are typically pre-programmed by experts, making visual augmentation static and inflexible. We introduce ShadAR, an AR system that allows users to describe expected visual augmentations (e.g., "Blur all people") for changing their vision in real time. ShadAR can graphically manipulate AR passthrough real-time via shader injection. When receiving a user’s prompt, ShadAR uses LLMs (GPT5.2) to interpret the user’s intent, analyzes the user’s view with object detection (YOLOv26), generates a pixel shader, and applies it to the targeted region on AR passthrough. To understand usage pattern, we invited 21 HCI researchers to use ShadAR, identifying four application domains (design, health, productivity, and social interaction) and two prompt-framing patterns: procedural prompts specifying what to modify and how (“Highlight the book.”), and end-goal prompts conveying desired mental/behavioral states (“Make me laugh.”). Such end-goal prompts suggest a future in which users specify outcomes (e.g., “Make me not miss my flight”) while the system determines how to realize them, though often with inherently indeterminate results. We discuss design opportunities for ShadAR and ethical concerns.
conference_title: ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology

title: Camera-Free Object Discovery and Interaction with GazeTags.
abstract: We present GazeTags, a camera- and computer-vision-free approach for worn head-gaze object awareness. Our small electronic tags cost roughly $2 each and can operate for more than a year on a coin cell battery. They work in concert with a user-worn device (smartglasses, hearables, etc.) that periodically emits a focused infrared signal aligned with the user’s head direction. Only GazeTags within that narrow head-oriented beam wake and respond, providing their identity and optional payloads such as object state or live sensor readings. By avoiding cameras and computer vision pipelines, our approach is very energy efficient, able to operate continuously even in battery-constrained wearables, and sidesteps non-trivial privacy issues. We describe our hardware design, characterize our system performance and operating tradeoffs, and demonstrate how GazeTags can enable practical gaze-aware environments.
conference_title: ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology

title: MorphoChrome: Interactive, Handheld Fabrication of Programmable Structural Color.
abstract: Surfaces that change color with viewing angle—from select butterfly wings and hummingbird feathers to passport holograms—communicate, authenticate, and display information without power or pigment. This is possible through structural color: vivid, view-dependent color produced by nanoscale geometry rather than pigment. However, existing methods for producing structural color are highly complex, lab-bound, and offer no direct user control over color output, color mixing, or angular encoding. We present MorphoChrome, a novel handheld optical system and workflow for interactive, programmable structural color fabrication. By exposing a holographic photopolymer film to user-controlled wavelengths and angles of coherent light, MorphoChrome directly inscribes the nanostructures required to produce iridescent color. Within the device, red, green, and blue laser diodes mix via optical beam combining to generate mixed color outputs. The device can be controlled either independently or through a digital twin user interface that provides physics-informed, live iridescent preview, and precise color selection for RGB color mixing. We evaluate MorphoChrome’s color gamut, color quality, resolution, and sub-second fabrication speed. We introduce a new resin-based adhesion process for integrating holographic films with 2D and 3D objects of diverse material composition (from PLA to fabric), and demonstrate a range of designs produced by our system through applications for colorimetric sensing, security, and biomimetic design.
conference_title: ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology

title: OpenGut: An Open-Source Platform for Gut-Computer Interaction Research.
abstract: Researchers are increasingly exploring the gut as a human-computer interface due to its gut-brain axis, linking physiological states with emotion and cognition. Despite its potential, the gut research space remains highly fragmented and underexplored. This is largely due to the absence of open and accessible hardware and software tools that could enable systematic investigation across disciplines and communities. To address this gap, we conducted semi-structured interviews with six experts to identify pain points in using existing platforms. Based on the themes identified, we formulated a set of requirements, and developed OpenGut, a rapid prototyping platform for gut research. Our open source platform consists of three main components: a wearable hardware platform for data capture and playback, a graphical user interface for visualization and analysis, as well as accompanying documentation for platform setup and customization. We perform technical evaluation of OpenGut for its signal quality, noise suppression, as well as outline potential usage scenarios for gut research.
conference_title: ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology

title: MoTUI: Personalization of In-Vehicle Tactile Interfaces for People With Vision Impairments and the Blind.
abstract: Configuring in-vehicle interfaces for people with vision impairments (VIPs) requires jointly tuning buttons, feedback modalities, layout, and speech parameters. This defines a design space too large for manual exploration, with inherently conflicting objectives such as maximizing situation awareness while minimizing cognitive load. Prior work recognizes personalization as critical but offers no systematic method to achieve it. We contribute MoTUI, an open-source Modular Tactile User Interface with reconfigurable hardware and software for runtime exploration of this design space and replication of existing designs. MoTUI is configuration-agnostic and supports multiple personalization strategies; we instantiate and evaluate one, pairing it with Human-in-the-Loop Multi-Objective Bayesian Optimization (HITL-MOBO) to navigate the space efficiently. In a within-subject study (N = 12 VIPs), HITL-optimized configurations outperformed a static baseline and an LLM-generated design on situation awareness, perceived workload, and satisfaction, with significant gains over the LLM-based approach. For psychological ownership, optimized configurations were rated significantly higher than both baselines. Importantly, optimization converged on substantially different configurations across participants, indicating strong individual differences; qualitative findings further explain these personalized outcomes.
conference_title: ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology

title: AtmoSteer: Personalized Scene Control with Reusable Atmospheric Recipes.
abstract: Generating scenes that convey atmospheres such as “cozy” or “contemplative” is difficult because people interpret them subjectively and often struggle to express them concretely. We present AtmoSteer, a human-in-the-loop approach that captures a user’s personal interpretation of an atmosphere as an atmospheric recipe: a weighted set of descriptive tags that can be reused across scenes for tasks such as image generation and image search. AtmoSteer supports users in discovering their own atmospheric recipes by exploring diverse interpretations with images and constructing a personalized vocabulary of visually grounded tags that describe style, layout, objects, and lighting. The system then supports preference refinement through two modes: slider-based weight adjustment of tags and visual example-based elicitation. In a user study on image generation (N=20), images generated from recipes produced by AtmoSteer were significantly more preferred and better aligned with participants’ subjective interpretations than those generated using generic descriptors or style transfer techniques.
conference_title: ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology

title: Graphionale: How Graph Visualizations of LLM Rationales Affect Human Decision Making.
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly equipped with augmented reasoning capabilities to generate rationales that support human decision-making. Yet these text-dense rationales often impose substantial cognitive burdens. Building on a formative co-design study that identified user preferences for non-linear reasoning representations, we developed Graphionale as a testbed for empirically studying argument-map-style rationale visualization. This system transforms linear LLM rationales into interactive, multi-level graphs. It explicitly structures logical relationships (e.g., conclusions, premises, support, and objections), while further extracting entities and relations within each statement to construct condensed node-link representations. We conduct a large-scale online user study (N = 204) to examine when graphical rationales are more effective than textual ones, across varying task modality (verbal vs. visual reasoning), rationale format (textual vs. graphical), and question difficulty (easy vs. hard). Our results show that graphical rationales do not help uniformly: they improve trust calibration for verbal reasoning yet feel more cognitively demanding and less satisfying; for visual reasoning, they impair calibration yet feel more engaging and helpful. In each modality, the format that better supports calibrated decisions is not the one users prefer, highlighting that matching rationale format to task modality is key to effective AI explanation design. Our findings contribute empirical design knowledge about when and how graphical rationales support human decision making, and inform the next-generation reasoning-aware AI interfaces.
conference_title: ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology

title: Remapping Time in Augmented Reality.
abstract: Video see-through augmented reality (VST AR) mediates the physical world through a camera capture–processing–display pipeline, making visual time computationally controllable. Yet this capability as a design consideration remains underexplored. We define and formalize time remapping as the intentional, real-time manipulation of how visual world time is presented to the user, and model it as a first-order dynamical system that balances delay accumulation and recovery. To evaluate its perceptual effectiveness, we conducted a within-subjects study (N = 21) in which participants identified briefly visible playing cards under baseline and remapped conditions, varying temporal anchor (self vs. external) and control (user vs. system). Time remapping approximately doubled identification accuracy without significantly reducing comfort, with gains consistent across all remapped conditions. Building on these findings and qualitative interviews, we derive a six-dimensional design space and instantiate it through three application prototypes. This paper establishes time remapping as a practical design material, introducing programmable time as a new dimension for AR experience design.
conference_title: ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology
